desc: Calprotectin is a neutrophil S100A8/S100A9 protein that starves microbes by chelating manganese and zinc, and serves as a stool biomarker of gut inflammation.

title: Irving–Williams Series
desc: The Irving–Williams series is the near-universal stability order of divalent transition-metal complexes: Mn<Fe<Co<Ni<Cu>Zn. Learn how it drives mismetallation.

title: Metal Intoxication
desc: Metal intoxication is nutritional immunity's offensive arm: hosts flood microbes with toxic copper and zinc to mismetalate enzymes and wreck Fe-S clusters.

title: Metal Sparing
desc: Metal sparing is the microbial response to metal starvation: swapping in isozymes that use a different metal, or none, to cut demand for the scarce metal.

title: Metallochaperone
desc: A metallochaperone is a soluble carrier protein that binds a specific metal ion and hands it directly to a target enzyme or transporter. How they work & why.

title: Metallome
desc: The metallome is the complete set of metal and metalloid species in a cell or organism — free ions plus every metal-bound biomolecule. Definition and role.

title: Metallomics
desc: Metallomics is the integrated study of the metallome: the identity, quantity, location, coordination and function of all metals in a biological system.

title: Metallophore
desc: A metallophore is a secreted low-molecular-weight chelator microbes use to scavenge scarce metals such as iron, copper, zinc, nickel, or cobalt.

title: Metalloproteome
desc: The metalloproteome is the complete set of metal-binding proteins in an organism — roughly a quarter to a half of all proteins. Definition and examples.

title: Metalloregulation
desc: Metalloregulation is how cells sense intracellular metal levels via metal-responsive proteins that switch genes on or off to maintain metal homeostasis.

title: Metallostasis
desc: Metallostasis is the cellular maintenance of metal-ion balance through sensing, buffering, trafficking, and sparing, keeping each metal's availability in range.

title: Mismetallation
desc: Mismetallation is when the wrong metal ion occupies a protein's active site, inactivating the enzyme — a core specificity problem microbes must prevent.

title: Nutritional Immunity

title: Enough metal. Available to whom?
desc: Enough metal. Available to whom? Start here · An organizing thesis The most useful question in microbial metallomics is not simply how much metal is present. It is which organism can reach which chemical form, in which compartment, with what effect on host and community. This is the field guide’s editorial framework: connect chemistry, microbial function, host regulation, and clinical outcomes, with each connection labeled by the evidence supporting it. An organizing thesis for microbial metallomics: chemical form, compartments, host–microbial competition, zinc and MS, iron restriction, and testable evidence gaps. Metal amount is not metal access A supplement label describes an input. A blood result samples a circulating pool. A microbiome report describes a community through the assay used to measure it. None, alone, tells us where the metal went, who used it, or whether that use helped the host. The central task is to connect these observations rather than substitute one for another. Iron makes the distinction concrete: hepcidin can reduce ferroportin-mediated export from cells, restricting delivery to the circulation. Zinc offers a different example: an inflammatory metal-binding protein can disadvantage susceptible microbes while a competitor with effective acquisition machinery retains an advantage. “Less available” always needs an answer to “available to whom?” Five questions to ask of every metal–microbe claim Question What must be specified A misleading shortcut Chemical form Ion, oxidation state, ligand, particle, or metal-containing molecule; dissolution and transformation. Treating every compound containing the same element as the same exposure. Local pool Gut lumen, mucosa, blood, tissue, or an intracellular compartment; bound versus exchangeable metal. Calling a low blood value a map of the entire body. Access machinery Transporters, binding molecules, efflux, host sequestration, and their activity in that setting. Assuming a detected gene is active or every strain has the same capacity. Biological function What changes: enzyme activity, respiration, competition, barrier function, or immune behavior? Treating a taxonomic shift as the mechanism itself. Host outcome Absorption, cellular use, inflammation, symptoms, and disease course are distinct endpoints. Calling any microbiome change harmful, or any absorption increase therapeutic. These are linked questions, not a validated equation or risk score. The proposed advance of this atlas is to keep the connections visible—and to mark the ones the evidence has not yet made. Nutritional immunity has a geography Host defense does not always mean removing a metal. In a macrophage model, ATP7A-dependent copper trafficking contributed to bacterial killing. In separate work, the bacterial ligand yersiniabactin buffered copper toxicity, and copper–yersiniabactin complexes were detected in human urinary infection samples. Metal delivery and microbial protection can therefore oppose one another. These studies do not constitute a single experiment tracing the same copper pool. Location can also change the result of the same dietary intervention. In mice, a manganese-rich diet worsened staphylococcal infection in the heart without the same pattern in liver and kidney. Subsequent work implicated altered neutrophil function as well. A story about feeding a bacterium can miss an effect on the cell trying to contain it. This is why “high” and “low” require a specimen, compartment, method, and comparison. Hypozincemia means low circulating zinc; it does not name zinc status inside every immune cell. A tissue elemental map is not a measurement of its labile, readily exchangeable intracellular pool. The spatial question belongs beside the concentration. Zinc: better absorption is only one connection Formulation matters, but the comparison matters just as much. A preliminary crossover study in eight healthy adults estimated greater zinc absorption from aspartate than from gluconate or sulfate when given with milk. It did not test oxide. A different 15-person trial found lower absorption from oxide than from citrate or gluconate under its own conditions. Combining their percentages into an aspartate-versus-oxide ranking would combine different experiments. Supported in a small human study Aspartate can change estimated host absorption. The absorption finding is real within the tested protocol. It is an endpoint about the host. Direct measurement of the zinc remaining in the gut, its chemical availability, and microbial acquisition before claiming that aspartate bypasses microbes. Preclinical signal · human mechanism unresolved Aspartate has a preclinical signal in an MS model. Oral zinc aspartate improved experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis in mice. A small human MS trial studied sulfate and depression; it found no between-group difference in the neurological examinations reported. A human formulation comparison with disease outcomes and evidence that a microbial zinc mechanism mediates any benefit. Calprotectin fits the question but does not answer it by itself. Its abundance is not a measurement of zinc occupancy, zinc flux, or which organism acquired the withheld metal. Likewise, an MS-associated microbial community does not reveal its zinc economy simply from the species names. Human cohort associations and experimental immune effects provide reasons to investigate, not proof of zinc theft. Read the zinc comparison, compartment map, and MS evidence ledger Iron: depleted stores and restricted delivery are different problems Absolute iron deficiency means stores are depleted. In inflammatory iron restriction, iron may be retained in storage and recycling cells while its delivery for red-cell production is constrained. Both can coexist. These are two mechanisms to distinguish, not an exhaustive classification of anemia. Human inflammatory signaling experiments and cellular ferroportin experiments explain a route from inflammation to reduced circulating iron. The attractive hypothesis is that oral iron can increase intestinal microbial exposure while host delivery remains limited. That is a question about competing destinations, not proof that every unsuccessful course of ferrous sulfate fed a pathogen. In an IBD trial, oral and intravenous treatment produced different microbial and metabolic changes, while both improved iron deficiency; changes in disease activity were not dependent on route. Counterevidence must be visible. A South African child trial improved iron status without detecting changes in the measured bacterial groups, short-chain fatty acids, or fecal calprotectin. Its setting and targeted assays matter. The defensible claim is that microbial effects vary with the population, formulation, background ecology, and endpoint—not that replacement is intrinsically harmful. Read the iron map: depletion, restriction, delivery, and formulation A disease signature must become a functional question A list of taxa is the beginning of a hypothesis, not the end of a mechanism. A higher relative abundance can reflect a fall in another population. Species labels do not establish transporter content, expression, access to substrate, or actual metal transfer. Quantitative microbiome profiling in MS shows why bacterial load and confounding can change which associations remain robust. Chemical selectivity can be very specific: gut bacterial transporters distinguish vitamin B12-related corrinoids. These are cobalt-containing molecules, not interchangeable supplies of free cobalt. Transporter mobility can also change competitive behavior within a gut microbial species. Functional capacity cannot safely be frozen into a permanent “good” or “bad” species label. The missing links between a signature and an intervention Evidence layer What it contributes What remains unproved Community association A reproducible association after diet, medication, stool characteristics, and absolute load are considered. That the organisms cause the disease or share one metal-handling phenotype. Functional potential Genes and pathways that could acquire, transform, exclude, or redistribute a metal. That they are expressed, chemically supplied, or important in this host. Activity and flux Evidence of expression, metabolites, local chemical pools, and movement between compartments. That changing this flux changes the clinical outcome. Causal and clinical effect An intervention changes the proposed pathway and a meaningful host endpoint. Whether that pathway mediates the host effect; generalization beyond the tested population, formulation, and setting. The next useful “signature” would join microbial functions to host regulation and metal chemistry in the same people over time. That is a research objective. This site does not currently possess a validated signature that selects a supplement for an individual. Make the thesis capable of being wrong A strong mechanism is not automatically a successful treatment rule. Hepcidin predicted use of oral iron in children, yet a later hepcidin-guided strategy that reduced iron exposure was less effective at improving hemoglobin and failed its prespecified non-inferiority test. Prediction and intervention answer different questions. Test access, not just abundance The zinc and iron literature suggests a shared measurement problem: host uptake, microbial exposure, and clinical benefit are usually studied separately. A useful clinical research comparison would connect them prospectively. Define the actual formulation, food context, route, and relevant host state before comparing outcomes. Measure host uptake or use alongside a defensible estimate of the local available metal pool; total stool concentration alone is insufficient. Track microbial functions and absolute community measures, with inflammation, medications, and baseline deficiency considered. Specify the host endpoint and the result that would contradict the proposed microbial mechanism before interpreting the data. If a formulation improves host uptake without changing the proposed microbial pathway, its benefit may be real while the microbial-bypass explanation is wrong. A change in the microbiome is also not a clinical endpoint by itself. In one mouse study, oral vitamin B12 changed distal-gut corrinoids and selected bacterial abundances without improving or worsening the measured colitis outcome. Null and discordant results help identify which part of a story actually explains the host. Use the atlas as a map of connections Read each profile in two directions: from the chemical form toward the host outcome, and backward from a disease observation toward the measurements needed to explain it. Zinc and iron are the first full worked examples of this approach. Across the broader atlas, distinguish a demonstrated mechanism from a plausible connection and a proposed test. title: Copper & microbes
desc: Cu Methane oxidation, copper acquisition, and metal toxicity Copper can be a microbial cofactor, a resource that requires specialized capture, and a stress imposed by the host. title: Iron & microbes
desc: Fe Iron stores, inflammatory restriction, microbial access, and formulation-dependent outcomes Iron is a nutrient, an enzyme cofactor, and an environmental electron acceptor. A useful microbial account must follow iron into local chemical pools, then connect acquisition and competition to host benefit or harm. Distinguish the pool from the delivery problem State Mechanistic picture Interpretive limit Absolute depletion Stores are reduced, limiting iron available for erythropoiesis. Inflammation can coexist; a single circulating result does not resolve the mixture. Inflammatory restriction IL-6 can increase hepcidin; hepcidin reduces ferroportin-mediated cellular export, limiting circulating delivery. This is regulated iron redistribution, not evidence that all iron in all tissues is excessive. The phrase “the body is trying to get iron out of the labile pool” needs a specified pool. Hepcidin–ferroportin biology concerns export and systemic availability; it is not a direct measurement of labile iron inside every cell. In a small marrow-characterized rheumatoid arthritis cohort, additional iron markers helped distinguish deficient stores and predict response—illustrating why the diagnostic question needs more than anemia alone. Depletion & restriction Oral iron: separate host response from microbial effects Randomized human route comparison Microbial change did not equal clinical worsening. In a trial including Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, and noninflamed iron-deficient controls, oral sulfate and intravenous sucrose produced distinct microbial and metabolic changes. Both improved iron deficiency; disease-activity changes were independent of route. A demonstrated causal chain from a particular iron-access function to a clinically important outcome. Randomized human counterexample Ferrous sulfate did not disrupt every measured community. In iron-deficient South African schoolchildren, supplementation improved iron status without detected changes in ten measured bacterial groups, fecal short-chain fatty acids, or calprotectin. Broader functional measurements and replication in other ecologies; a targeted null result is not proof of no possible effect. These findings sit beside the Kenyan infant fortification studies above. Different baseline ecology, age, formulation, and measurement scope can produce different results. It is plausible that unabsorbed iron supports some organisms, but identifying that path requires more than a poor hemoglobin response or an increase in relative abundance. Host feedback also changes exposure over time. Stable-isotope studies in iron-depleted women found that oral sulfate increased hepcidin and reduced absorption of a subsequent dose. The fraction absorbed and the absolute amount absorbed are different quantities. Timing is part of the mechanism; this experiment does not provide a microbiome-based dosing rule. Host & microbial outcomes A formulation can matter without proving microbial exclusion The IHAT-GUT phase II trial randomized 642 young Gambian children to iron hydroxide adipate tartrate, ferrous sulfate, or placebo. IHAT met the trial’s non-inferiority criterion for the composite efficacy endpoint. The rate of moderate-to-severe diarrhea was lower than with sulfate, while the proportion experiencing at least one such episode was similar. These are different safety measures. Interpret the comparison at its actual scale: phase II, different elemental doses selected for estimated comparable bioavailability, and 80% confidence intervals. The result supports further formulation research; it does not prove general superiority or establish that a particular pathogen was denied iron. Formulation evidence The decisive question is where replacement goes Measure host use and microbial exposure together A stronger study would distinguish failure to absorb, restricted export, inadequate stores, ongoing losses, and microbial competition instead of assigning every weak response to the microbiome. Characterize iron stores and inflammatory context, accounting for mixed states. Measure host incorporation or a meaningful hematologic response alongside the local iron species accessible to microbes. Connect microbial acquisition functions and metabolites to absolute community changes, rather than treat a taxonomic list as a flux measurement. Judge the formulation using host efficacy and clinical adverse outcomes as well as microbial endpoints. If host response improves with no change in the proposed microbial function, that function is not established as the mediator. A final caution against overconfident precision: hepcidin predicted oral iron utilization in one study, but a later hepcidin-guided child trial reduced iron exposure at the cost of a worse hemoglobin response and failed non-inferiority. The assembled evidence does not establish that ordinary zinc oxide supplementation worsens MS, or that aspartate helps human MS by denying zinc to microbes. Those are hypotheses with several missing connections, not interchangeable summaries of these studies. MS evidence ledger What would discriminate the explanations? Pair host absorption with microbial access A useful formulation comparison would test whether the putative advantage is improved host uptake, changed local microbial access, an immune effect, or some combination. The existing absorption and EAE studies do not distinguish these explanations. Use a direct comparison in the same population and food context, with matched interpretation of elemental input and host uptake. Characterize residual intestinal zinc chemistry alongside microbial acquisition functions; species abundance alone is insufficient. Keep calprotectin, circulating zinc, microbial function, and clinical outcomes as separate measurements. For MS, account for disease-modifying treatment and assess a prespecified clinical endpoint rather than infer benefit from a microbiome shift. If host uptake improves but microbial access does not change, reject the bypass explanation without discarding the absorption result. Discriminating the mechanisms

title: Scandium & microbes
desc: Sc Modulation of bacterial gene expression Scandium can alter bacterial gene expression and the production of extracellular enzymes and secondary metabolites. It is a rare-earth element, but not a lanthanide. The evidence here concerns a culture condition that changes microbial behavior, rather than an established scandium-containing enzyme or a universal nutritional requirement. Rare earth Secondary metabolism Gene expression Bacterial culture Streptomyces coelicolor A3(2)

title: Rubidium & microbes
desc: Rb Transport through potassium-handling systems Rubidium is useful for understanding how bacteria distinguish chemically similar alkali-metal ions. It can enter through potassium-handling systems and can partly substitute for potassium under some culture conditions. Transportability, however, is not the same as physiological equivalence: the transporter, strain, and potassium background change the result. Alkali metal Potassium transport Ion selectivity Bacterial culture E. coli potassium transport systems

title: Americium & microbes
desc: Am Microbial accumulation and biosorption Americium research in microbes is mainly about binding and partitioning rather than a demonstrated biological redox cycle. Bacteria, fungal biomass, and dissolved microbial products can change how americium distributes between water, cells, and mineral surfaces. Actinide Radionuclide Biosorption Fungal biomass Environmental microbiology Immobilized Rhizopus arrihizus; laboratory solutions

title: Yttrium & microbes
desc: Y Binding to microbial biomass Yttrium has direct microbial evidence for biosorption and for recognition by a selective metal-binding protein. Neither observation establishes that bacteria require yttrium for growth. Although grouped with the rare-earth elements, yttrium is not a lanthanide, and its biology should be evaluated on its own evidence. Rare earth Biosorption Wastewater Metal recovery Serratia marcescens biomass

title: Follow the metal.
desc: Follow the metal. A qualitative mechanism explorer Choose a case. Trace the compartments. Find the connection that still needs evidence. These diagrams organize findings from distinct studies. Arrows describe a proposed route through the question; they do not mean that every step has been demonstrated in one experiment. There are no calculated doses or predicted patient outcomes. Explore zinc absorption, iron restriction, copper defense, and corrinoid selection through sourced compartment diagrams and explicit missing evidence. Zinc · absorption and competition Human absorption + separate microbial models Does more zinc reach the host—or less reach the microbes? One input, two access questions Formulation in the gut Aspartate, oxide, sulfate, and gluconate are formulation labels. The human comparisons tested different subsets under different food and measurement conditions. Host branch · uptake A higher absorbed fraction describes entry into the host. It does not identify how much remaining zinc is usable by a particular gut organism. Microbial branch · local access Calprotectin and microbial acquisition machinery can change competition in an inflamed niche. This was studied separately from the human formulation comparisons. The tempting inference is that better host absorption leaves less zinc for microbes. That may change total residual exposure, but chemical accessibility, timing, and location still need measurement. “Aspartate bypasses microbes” remains an untested explanation in the evidence assembled here. Open the formulation and MS evidence ledger Iron · stores and delivery Cellular mechanism + human intervention evidence The dose enters the gut. Does usable iron reach the marrow? Separate entry, export, and use Intestinal exposure Oral replacement introduces iron into the lumen. Its microbial and metabolic effects can differ from intravenous delivery. Host export Hepcidin binding to ferroportin reduces cellular iron export. Iron can be retained while circulating delivery falls. Red-cell production Hemoglobin response is a host outcome, not a direct readout of microbial feeding. A biomarker-guided reduction in exposure did not preserve efficacy in one child trial. First distinguish depleted stores, inflammatory restriction, and mixtures. Even in inflammatory bowel disease, depleted stores can accompany low hepcidin. Inflammation does not guarantee a closed export gate in every patient. Open the iron depletion and restriction map Copper · delivery and buffering Distinct cellular, chemical, and human-specimen studies A metal delivered as a defense can meet a microbial buffer. Opposing processes, assembled across studies Host trafficking A macrophage study implicated ATP7A-dependent copper delivery in antibacterial activity. Microbial ligand Yersiniabactin binds copper and can protect bacteria from its toxicity. Infection compartment Copper–yersiniabactin complexes were detected in human urinary infection specimens. Detection does not establish their contribution to each patient’s severity. The missing connection is simultaneous measurement of host delivery, ligand-bound versus accessible copper, and the host outcome in the same setting. A total copper result cannot supply all three. These studies do not establish that changing dietary copper would reproduce either mechanism. Read the copper profile Cobalt · molecule and transporter Gut bacterial mechanisms + a mouse supplementation study The cobalt atom does not tell you who can use the molecule. Chemical identity meets selective access Corrinoid mixture Vitamin B12 and related corrinoids contain cobalt. Their molecular differences matter to microbial use. Transporter repertoire Multiple transporters can discriminate among analogs; transferable transport capacity can change competition within a species. Community and host Oral B12 altered distal-gut corrinoids and some bacterial abundances in mice without changing the measured colitis outcome. The transporter studies have not shown that transporter selectivity caused the separate supplementation-associated community shift. Nor do they establish whether a particular community’s corrinoid handling limits host benefit in a defined clinical setting. Free cobalt supplementation is not an equivalent intervention. Read the cobalt profile

title: Divine Aleru
desc: Divine Aleru translates microbiome research into structured evidence and accessible scientific writing. Her work centers on the interpretation of microbial signatures, study design and disease context, helping readers compare findings across studies and understand what the evidence can support. Microbial signatures Evidence synthesis Disease-associated microbiomes Medical writing Open science Making microbial signatures comparable across studies Aleru contributes to BugSigDB’s organization of published microbiome signatures through Bioconductor’s Outreachy program. Her project account describes curation of glucose-metabolism studies and contributions to R-based analysis. This work helps turn scattered findings into structured records that retain information about the study, condition and microbial pattern. Comparing microbiome and metallomic signatures first requires knowing whether the microbial patterns are comparable at all. Curation provides that foundation: it makes differences in body site, population and study context visible, helping future metal-focused analyses avoid treating every reported association as the same biological signal. The next step is to connect curated signatures to measured exposures and microbial functions while keeping association, mechanistic interpretation and clinical validation explicitly separate. Bioconductor — Aleru’s BugSigDB curation and analysis account Bioconductor — Annual report documenting the Outreachy cohort

title: Ryszard Łobiński
desc: Develops analytical approaches for detecting, identifying and quantifying trace-metal species in biological and environmental systems. His work helped establish metallomics and links mass spectrometry, chemical speciation and systems microbiology. Mass spectrometry Speciation Metalloproteomics Turning an elemental signal into an identified biological compound Łobiński has developed analytical approaches that combine element-specific detection with molecular mass spectrometry. Work identifying previously unknown selenium metabolites in enriched yeast illustrates the contribution: finding selenium in a sample becomes a starting point for determining which molecules contain it and how microbial metabolism has transformed it. This gives microbial metallomics a way to test claims about chemical form. It is especially relevant when foods or supplements contain products of microbial metabolism: the same total amount of an element can be distributed among different compounds that require separate identification and biological evaluation. The frontier is to improve identification and quantification across the full sample while retaining evidence about which compounds survive digestion, enter tissues or remain accessible to microbes. Dernovics, Far and Łobiński — Identification of anionic selenium species in selenium-rich yeast

title: Dietrich H. Nies
desc: Investigates how bacteria maintain metal balance in highly contaminated environments. Work with Cupriavidus metallidurans and its metal-efflux systems has helped explain how microbes tolerate metals and transform their surrounding chemistry. Metal resistance Efflux Cupriavidus Made mixed-metal toxicity a mechanistic problem Nies and colleagues studied how Cupriavidus metallidurans survives metal-rich environments and transforms gold compounds. Their work showed that copper and gold can interact toxically because gold interferes with copper export. The biological response to a mixture therefore differed from what separate measurements of either metal would suggest. This is a direct reason to take environmental metallomics seriously: one contaminant can disturb the handling of another element. Nies’s work connects microbial tolerance, metal transformation, and mixture effects. It provides a mechanistic basis for asking what contamination does to microbial function, beyond documenting that metals are present. The next challenge is determining which mixture interactions matter at environmental concentrations and how microbial transformation changes exposure over time in soils, water, and other communities. Wiesemann and colleagues, Copper–gold mixture toxicity (2017) Bütof and colleagues, Copper–gold detoxification and biomineralisation (2018)

title: John D. Helmann
desc: Uses Bacillus subtilis to study cellular responses to metal deficiency, metal excess, reactive oxygen species and antibiotics. His laboratory examines transcriptional regulation and the molecular sensors that coordinate these stress responses. Bacillus Metal sensors Oxidative stress Revealed that microbes reorganize their metal budgets Helmann’s work connects metal-sensing regulators to coordinated physiological responses. In Bacillus subtilis, studies of zinc-responsive ribosomal proteins showed how alternative proteins help sustain growth during zinc scarcity. The ribosome participates in the metal economy: a cell can change how it allocates zinc while preserving essential protein synthesis. For microbial metallomics, this explains why a change in metal supply can alter cellular priorities before it stops growth. Taxonomic abundance alone may miss that transition. Helmann’s research directs attention to resource allocation and stress responses when interpreting what nutritional immunity or environmental metal scarcity is doing to a community. A useful next step is to track metal allocation and expressed functions alongside community composition, establishing which adaptations remain active in complex, changing environments. Gabriel and Helmann, Zinc-responsive ribosomal proteins (2009) Cornell research profile

title: Gemma Reguera
desc: Studies how microbes adapt to environmental change and applies that knowledge to bioremediation, bioenergy and nanotechnology. Her group investigates electroactive microbes, microbial communities that remove agrochemicals, and the behavior of human-associated microbiomes. Geobacter Bioenergy Bioremediation Explaining how contaminant removal and microbial survival connect Reguera’s group linked extracellular uranium reduction in Geobacter to protection of the bacterial cell. Their work found that uranium immobilization outside the cell was associated with preserved respiratory activity and viability, connecting the location of a metal transformation to the organism’s ability to sustain that transformation. Her contribution makes bioremediation a biological performance question as well as a chemical one. A community must keep functioning while it encounters a contaminant. For microbial metallomics, the location of metal deposition and the physiology of participating cells help explain whether removal can continue. The next question is how these protective processes operate in heterogeneous field communities and whether contaminant immobilization remains effective as environmental conditions change over time. Cologgi et al. — Extracellular uranium reduction as a protective cellular mechanism Michigan State — Reguera research profile

title: Walter J. Chazin
desc: Uses structural biology and biophysics to connect protein structure, dynamics and function. His metal-biology work includes the host-defense protein calprotectin and the molecular basis of antimicrobial metal sequestration. Calprotectin Structural biology Nutritional immunity Explaining how an immune protein captures a metal Chazin and colleagues resolved the molecular basis of manganese sequestration by calprotectin, linking its unusual metal-binding architecture to antimicrobial activity. This structural work explains how a host protein can compete for a nutrient that microbes need, rather than treating calprotectin only as a marker of inflammation. His contribution gives nutritional immunity a chemical mechanism that can be measured and challenged. For this field, a protein concentration alone is insufficient: its binding sites, metal occupancy and surrounding chemistry determine whether it actually changes the metal available to microbes. An important next step is to connect these molecular binding properties to the metal species and protein states present in individual human tissues during inflammation. Damo et al. — Molecular basis for manganese sequestration by calprotectin

title: David P. Giedroc
desc: Investigates how bacteria sense and manage metals, reactive sulfur species and oxidative stress. His laboratory combines structural biology, spectroscopy and biochemistry to explain the regulatory switches that keep essential metal chemistry under control. Metallostasis Metal sensors Sulfur biology Revealed how metal binding becomes a regulatory signal Giedroc’s research explains the molecular switches by which bacteria respond to metals. Work on the zinc sensor CzrA showed that zinc changes the protein’s internal motions and weakens DNA binding, even without a dramatic overall structural change. Metal detection is therefore a dynamic communication process within a protein. His work fills the gap between a metal entering a cell and that cell changing its behavior. For microbial metallomics, knowing that a metal binds is insufficient: researchers must establish whether binding triggers the correct response. That distinction helps explain why metal balance depends on functional regulation. The translational question is whether metal-sensing responses can be altered selectively enough to have useful biological effects, while accounting for different regulatory systems in host and community members. Capdevila and colleagues, Entropy redistribution in a metalloregulatory protein (2017) Giedroc Group, Indiana University

title: Deborah B. Zamble †
desc: Investigated how bacteria acquire and deliver nickel to enzymes, including the metallochaperones involved in hydrogenase maturation. Her work helped explain the coordination between metal sensing, transport and enzyme assembly. This historical entry commemorates her contributions. Nickel Hydrogenases Chaperones Explained how bacteria select and deliver nickel Zamble’s research established molecular connections among bacterial nickel sensing, acquisition, and enzyme maturation. Her group studied how nickel-delivery proteins recognize the metal and interact with one another, including work on the changing nickel-binding environments of the hydrogenase maturation proteins HypA and HypB. Nickel utilization emerged as a coordinated cellular process. Her contribution is fundamental to understanding why nickel exposure affects organisms differently. An enzyme’s dependence on nickel does not mean all nickel in its surroundings can activate it. The sensing and delivery machinery helps determine usable supply, giving microbial metallomics a functional explanation beyond simply listing nickel-dependent species. The continuing question is how nickel delivery operates under the chemical constraints of real host niches, and whether that knowledge supports selective, validated therapeutic approaches. University of Toronto, scientific remembrance of Deborah Zamble Lacasse and colleagues, Nickel binding by HypA (2019)

title: Valeria C. Culotta
desc: Investigates how metals and reactive oxygen species shape the interaction between hosts and fungal pathogens. Her laboratory studies copper, manganese, iron and superoxide dismutases, with particular attention to Candida albicans and Candida auris. Copper Manganese Fungal pathogens Showed that infection changes metal geography Culotta and colleagues demonstrated that copper availability changes during experimental Candida infection and that the fungus adjusts its antioxidant enzymes accordingly. In the mouse model, rising serum copper did not describe the changing copper conditions in infected kidneys. The organism switched between copper- and manganese-dependent forms of superoxide dismutase. Her work makes a crucial point explicit: a blood metal measurement need not report the environment experienced by a microbe in tissue. It also shows why nutritional immunity is dynamic. A pathogen’s metal requirements and defenses can change during infection, complicating simple assumptions about supplementing or withholding one element. The next clinical bridge is to measure these local metal states and fungal responses during human infection, then determine which findings predict meaningful treatment outcomes. Li and colleagues, Candida adaptation to host copper (2015) Johns Hopkins, Culotta Lab

title: Joanna Szpunar
desc: Develops high-resolution mass-spectrometry approaches for metal, metalloid and biomolecule speciation. The FTMS Bio platform she leads applies Fourier-transform mass spectrometry to environmental and health questions, including molecular identification and quantitative analysis. Mass spectrometry Speciation Selenium Making the composition of microbial nutrient products testable Szpunar’s analytical work distinguishes selenium-containing proteins, metabolites and inorganic forms in enriched yeast. A study with Bierla and Łobiński developed quantification of protein-associated selenocysteine alongside other selenium pools, addressing the problem of assigning an element accurately among the compounds present in a microbial product. This is directly useful for evaluating what a microbial food or supplement actually contains. It replaces an undifferentiated selenium claim with chemical evidence and supports meaningful comparisons between products, preparations and studies before those differences are interpreted as differences in bioavailability or health effects. The next step is to connect well-characterized product composition to transformations during digestion and to measured host and microbial outcomes, rather than assuming composition alone predicts benefit. Bierla, Łobiński and Szpunar — Determination of proteinaceous selenocysteine in selenized yeast UPPA — FTMS Bio speciation platform

title: Thomas V. O'Halloran
desc: Investigates the cell biology and coordination chemistry of metals, including intracellular metal trafficking, zinc dynamics and copper homeostasis. His work on metallochaperones helped explain how cells deliver reactive metal ions to the proteins that need them. Copper Zinc Metal trafficking Established that metals require directed intracellular delivery O’Halloran and collaborators helped establish the metallochaperone concept. Their work on the yeast protein Atx1 identified a soluble copper receptor that interacts with a copper-trafficking partner. This supplied a molecular explanation for how cells can route a reactive, potentially toxic ion toward the proteins that need it. The contribution changes what metal sufficiency means. Copper entering a cell does not guarantee that it reaches the appropriate destination. Microbial metallomics must therefore examine delivery pathways as well as transport and total abundance—a principle that connects nutrient utilization, cellular dysfunction, and the interpretation of metal exposure. A key frontier is determining when altered trafficking, rather than altered total copper, explains a biological phenotype and how that distinction can be measured reliably. Pufahl and colleagues, Atx1 copper chaperone function (1997) O’Halloran laboratory publication record

title: Kimberly Eyer
desc: Co-founder of ICS and a member of its executive leadership, with a public record as a co-author of certification standards. Her Microbiome Medicine profile describes a professional nursing background. She is a co-author on research records featured in this guide. Standards Microbiome research Translation Connecting evidence communication with accountable standards work Eyer’s documented contributions combine certification-standard co-authorship and institutional leadership with research curation and writing at Microbiome Medicine. Her public profile describes a nursing background. This places her contribution at the interface of evidence communication and practical standards, where research findings must be translated into clear, documented requirements. Microbial metallomics needs people who can make complex findings understandable and preserve the distinction between an observation, a proposed explanation and an actionable standard. This work can help audiences follow the evidence while making responsibility for institutional claims and certification decisions visible. The next translation task is to show how a standard’s requirements follow from evidence, how uncertainty is handled and whether implementation produces the intended measurable outcomes. Institute of Contaminant Standards — Eyer’s published role and standards co-authorship Microbiome Medicine — Eyer author record

title: Stéphane L. Benoit
desc: Investigates nickel acquisition, storage and nickel-dependent enzymes in bacterial pathogens. His work on Helicobacter and Campylobacter connects hydrogenase and urease biology with host colonization, respiratory metabolism and iron–sulfur protein maturation. He has also explored nickel chelation against multidrug-resistant enteric bacteria in laboratory and animal-model studies. Nickel Hydrogenases & urease Microbial pathogenesis Nickel chelation Turning bacterial nickel dependence into an antimicrobial target. Benoit and colleagues showed that dimethylglyoxime (DMG), a nickel chelator, inhibited growth of tested multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhimurium and Klebsiella pneumoniae strains. Separate mouse and insect experiments supplied evidence of biological benefit. A Campylobacter jejuni study showed that metal interactions can change the antimicrobial response. These findings give experimental grounding to the idea that access to an enzyme cofactor can be a therapeutic research target. His work connects the chemistry of an enzyme cofactor with the urgent search for antimicrobials. A pathogen’s metal-dependent functions can reveal targets that its conventional antibiotic-resistance profile does not describe. This is a central promise of microbial metallomics: understanding the chemistry a microbe relies on can suggest a new way to alter its behavior. Benoit and colleagues supplied experimental grounding for pursuing that direction. The next research question is where nickel-directed approaches offer a useful and selective effect in the biological settings that matter. Explaining which aspects of metal handling predict response—and which predict failure—would turn a promising proof of concept into a more informative therapeutic strategy. Host effects and the wider microbial community belong in that explanation from the beginning. Benoit et al. (2019) — Nickel chelation therapy as an approach to combat multi-drug resistant enteric pathogens Benoit & Maier — DMG and copper toxicity in Campylobacter jejuni (2022) DMG shows why the mechanism deserves attention Tested enteric bacterial strains · laboratory studies DMG was bacteriostatic against tested Salmonella Typhimurium and Klebsiella pneumoniae, including multidrug-resistant strains. Nickel-dependent enzyme activities were inhibited. Growth inhibition and reduced enzyme activity connect metal access to bacterial function: a starting point for a different antimicrobial strategy. Mouse and insect infection models · 2019 Separate mouse experiments reported improved survival and lower organ burdens in Salmonella infection. Preventive insect experiments reported protection against the tested multidrug-resistant Salmonella and Klebsiella. The biological benefit extends beyond a culture dish and gives the therapeutic concept a reason to advance into further investigation. Campylobacter jejuni · laboratory study, 2022 DMG inhibited growth. Its combination with copper was bactericidal under the tested conditions; the combined effect did not generalize to selected other Gram-negative bacteria. Metal interactions can change the outcome. Organism-specific responses create an opportunity to explain when the same chemical intervention behaves differently. Why this belongs in the antimicrobial-resistance conversation WHO’s 2024 list prioritizes defined pathogen–resistance combinations for research and investment. Benoit’s work belongs in that conversation because it investigates a different therapeutic concept: restricting access to a cofactor that bacterial functions require. The findings provide a starting point for asking how widely that principle applies. The WHO list establishes the public-health priority; the biochemical and infection studies below establish the mechanistic rationale. WHO — Bacterial Priority Pathogens List, 2024 Where nickel biology meets WHO research priorities Several organisms represented in the WHO list have published nickel-enzyme biology relevant to this question. These selected examples connect a public-health priority with a biochemical or infection finding; they are not a complete enzyme census, and the cited studies do not all examine the specific resistant strains named by WHO. Published starting points for a nickel-directed antimicrobial hypothesis Klebsiella pneumoniae Critical: carbapenem-resistant and third-generation-cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales. Nickel-dependent urease activity and bacterial growth were inhibited in the DMG study, including work with multidrug-resistant isolates. An existing proof of concept connects nickel restriction with loss of a bacterial function. Benoit et al. (2019) Salmonella Typhimurium High: fluoroquinolone-resistant nontyphoidal Salmonella. Respiratory hydrogen use was linked to virulence in a mouse study. The later DMG study reported inhibition of nickel-dependent hydrogenase activity. Metal access connects an energy pathway to infection biology, providing a reason to investigate nickel-directed approaches. Maier et al. (2004) Benoit et al. (2019) Escherichia coli Critical: carbapenem-resistant and third-generation-cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales. The characterized glyoxalase I was most active with nickel and inactive with zinc; other metals also supported activity in biochemical assays. Human glyoxalase I uses zinc. Different metal activation creates a rationale for investigating selective disruption of bacterial methylglyoxal detoxification. Nickel exclusivity in a host is a further question. He et al. (2000) Pseudomonas aeruginosa High: carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa. PAO1 contains three characterized glyoxalase I homologs: two in the Ni/Co-activated class and one in the zinc-dependent class. Multiple metal-activation classes make this an informative case for asking whether alternative enzyme activity changes the response to nickel restriction. Sukdeo & Honek (2007) Staphylococcus aureus High: methicillin-resistant S. aureus. Urease, an established nickel-dependent enzyme, contributed to acid-response physiology and persistent kidney infection in mice. A metal-dependent function is connected to persistence in a host: a rationale for investigating nickel access in that setting. This study did not test DMG. Zhou et al. (2019) The mechanism is the reason to investigate If an infection-relevant function needs nickel, and an intervention restricts the nickel pool that supplies it, that function may become a therapeutic vulnerability even when conventional antibiotics fail. This is the research hypothesis. Benoit’s work matters because it connects that biochemical idea with observed antimicrobial effects. A chelator’s affinity is part of the argument. Biological activity also depends on which nickel pool it can reach and how that pool supplies the relevant enzyme. Restricting access during enzyme assembly is a different proposition from extracting nickel already bound inside an active enzyme. Following those connections is how microbial metallomics turns a chemical property into a biological explanation. An enzyme name starts the question “Glyoxalase I positive” is not synonymous with nickel-dependent: distinct metal-activation classes exist. Likewise, the nickel-bearing hydrogenases are the [NiFe] class; other hydrogenase classes use iron without nickel. Enzyme presence, its actual cofactor, its activity in a host, and its contribution to infection are separate links in the argument. A metabolic function can matter for stress survival or persistence without already having been established as a virulence factor in every organism. Identifying that missing connection is valuable foundational science. It gives a promising idea a specific next question instead of treating the absence of a completed chain as a reason to stop. Sukdeo & Honek (2007) — Glyoxalase I metal classes Caserta et al. (2023) — Assembly of a [NiFe]-hydrogenase active site Peters et al. (1998) — An iron-only hydrogenase structure What would move the explanation forward? The mechanistic prediction is a relationship between altered nickel availability, reduced activity of the proposed nickel-dependent function, and a meaningful biological effect. A response explained equally well by unrelated toxicity would support a different account. A relevant function sustained through another metal or pathway would help explain limited response. These alternatives make the hypothesis more informative. The larger opportunity is to connect pathogen biology, the host’s metal regulation, and the surrounding community. A community’s metal-handling functions may reveal dependencies that a species list or an antibiotic-resistance label leaves invisible. Establishing which of those dependencies matter is a research agenda for microbiome medicine—and a reason these pioneers deserve attention.

title: Katherine J. Franz
desc: Investigates how biological systems manage the coordination chemistry of essential but potentially toxic metals, especially copper and iron. Her laboratory develops chemical tools to change metal location, speciation and reactivity, including approaches relevant to microbial pathogens. Copper Iron Chemical biology Connected metal availability to antifungal drug response Franz and colleagues showed in laboratory Candida cultures that exposure to fluconazole changes the organism’s sensitivity to copper availability. Their chemical analyses distinguished this biological interaction from simply forming a copper–drug complex. The result links an established antifungal drug’s effects to the metal conditions surrounding the treated cells. This points to a concrete opportunity for metallomics in medicine: the chemical environment can influence how a drug performs. Franz’s work gives researchers a way to examine metal–drug interactions mechanistically, including location and speciation, before assuming that adding a metal or a chelator will improve treatment. The next translational question is whether these interactions persist in infected tissues with acceptable host safety and demonstrable clinical benefit; laboratory growth effects alone cannot establish that. Hunsaker and Franz, Copper and azole antifungal activity (2019) Duke research profile

title: Lucia Banci
desc: Uses structural biology and NMR to study metal ions, protein maturation and intracellular metal trafficking. Her group developed in-cell NMR approaches that allow proteins to be examined in living cells at atomic resolution. NMR Metal trafficking Structural biology Observed metalloprotein maturation inside living cells Banci and colleagues developed in-cell NMR approaches that resolve protein chemistry within living human cells. In work on superoxide dismutase 1, they followed zinc binding, protein assembly, and copper uptake at atomic resolution. This made metal-dependent maturation observable in the cellular setting where the protein actually functions. Her contribution helps close a central measurement gap: detecting an element and detecting a protein do not prove that the protein contains the right metal or has matured correctly. The methods offer microbial metallomics and host metal biology a way to test functional metalation rather than infer it. The frontier is extending such measurements to more proteins and physiologically relevant conditions, so altered metalation can be distinguished from changes in protein abundance or total metal. Banci and colleagues, Protein maturation in live human cells (2013) CERM scientific profile

title: Hiroki Haraguchi
desc: Proposed metallomics as an integrated field for studying metals and metal-containing biomolecules. His foundational 2004 paper connects elemental analysis and chemical speciation with the questions raised by genomics and proteomics. Metallomics Elemental analysis Speciation Gave metals a place beside genes and proteins Haraguchi proposed metallomics as a field integrating the study of metals with genomics and proteomics. His foundational paper made chemical speciation central: identifying the metal-containing molecules that perform biological work, rather than treating an elemental measurement as a complete account of metal biology. This is the organizing idea behind microbial metallomics. A microbial gene inventory cannot establish which metal-dependent reactions are operating. Haraguchi’s framework asks researchers to connect elements, their molecular partners, and biological function—the bridge needed between microbiome sequencing and a chemically informed account of health or exposure. The continuing challenge is to measure metal-containing molecules in complex microbial communities while preserving their chemical identities and linking those measurements to expressed biological functions. Haraguchi, Metallomics as integrated biometal science (2004)

title: James A. Imlay
desc: Studies how reactive oxygen species damage bacteria and how cells defend themselves. His work connects oxidative stress with iron-containing enzymes, metal availability and the repair or protection of vulnerable metabolic pathways. Oxidative stress Iron Enzyme damage Demonstrated how the wrong metal disables metabolism Imlay and Gu showed that oxidative stress can remove iron from bacterial enzymes, after which zinc occupies the vacated sites and supports little activity. The proteins need not be destroyed for metabolism to fail. Their experiments made mismetallation a demonstrated mechanism connecting oxidative stress, competing metals, and enzyme dysfunction. This is why mismetallation matters to the field. An essential nutrient can become harmful in the wrong molecular position, and the same exposure may act differently when oxidative stress changes the competition. Imlay’s work provides a concrete alternative to treating every metal-associated effect as generalized toxicity or deficiency. The next challenge is identifying which enzymes are mismetallated in real host-associated communities and linking their altered occupancy to function at relevant exposure levels. Gu and Imlay, Superoxide-induced mismetallation (2013) Imlay Lab research overview

title: Manuela Raffatellu
desc: Studies the competition between intestinal pathogens and the microbiota. Her research connects Salmonella colonization, inflammation and nutrient acquisition, including the ways host iron- and metal-withholding defenses reshape microbial competition in the gut. Salmonella Gut microbiome Nutritional immunity Showing how nutritional immunity reshapes competition in the gut Raffatellu and collaborators demonstrated that calprotectin-driven zinc restriction can favor Salmonella over competing gut microbes in an inflamed mouse intestine. Her laboratory also studies competition for iron and other nutrients, connecting the host response to the relative success of pathogens and resident community members. This supplies a crucial ecological correction to the idea that withholding a metal affects all microbes equally. The outcome depends on which organisms can still acquire it. Her work makes community competition central to evaluating nutritional immunity and proposed interventions that alter microbial metal access. The translational question is whether metal-dependent competition can be shifted reproducibly in human communities, with benefits demonstrated beyond a change in the abundance of a selected microbe. Liu et al. — Zinc sequestration and Salmonella growth in the inflamed gut Raffatellu laboratory — Nutritional immunity and microbial competition

title: Joseph A. Cotruvo Jr.
desc: Studies how bacteria recognize, acquire and use rare-earth elements. Research on the lanthanide-binding protein lanmodulin links microbial metal selectivity with protein engineering and opportunities for biological rare-earth separation. Lanthanides Lanmodulin Metal recovery Turned microbial metal selectivity into a separation principle Cotruvo and colleagues discovered lanmodulin, a bacterial protein that recognizes lanthanides with striking selectivity over calcium. Subsequent collaborative work demonstrated rare-earth recovery from mixtures using the protein. The research connects a microorganism’s ability to discriminate among elements with practical approaches to detecting and recovering strategically important metals. This is a concrete example of microbial metallomics producing useful chemistry beyond clinical medicine. Understanding how organisms select scarce elements can inform resource recovery and environmental measurement. It also demonstrates why metal-binding specificity deserves direct study: chemically similar or abundant competing ions need not have equivalent biological access. The frontier is translating molecular selectivity into robust recovery and sensing systems for variable real-world materials, while evaluating performance, reuse, and environmental costs at larger scales. Cotruvo and colleagues, Discovery of lanmodulin (2018) Deblonde and colleagues, Rare-earth extraction using lanmodulin (2020)

title: Caryn E. Outten
desc: Studies how cells sense and distribute iron, with an emphasis on iron–sulfur clusters and glutaredoxin proteins. Her research connects the chemistry of these cofactors with iron regulation, redox balance and cellular stress. Iron–sulfur clusters Glutaredoxins Redox biology Explained how iron-containing cofactors report cellular iron status Outten’s research links iron–sulfur cluster handling to the regulation of iron metabolism. Work in yeast established molecular details of cluster exchange between glutaredoxin–BolA proteins and the iron regulator Aft2. This connects the assembly and movement of an iron-containing cofactor with the cell’s decision to mobilize more iron. The implication for microbial metallomics is that iron sensing is integrated with iron utilization. A cell’s response cannot be understood solely from its total iron content. Outten’s work connects cofactor delivery, redox biology, and nutrient regulation, providing mechanisms for studying functional iron disruption in microbial and host cells. A continuing question is when disrupted cluster handling produces an apparent cellular iron need despite available iron, and how to distinguish that state from simple scarcity. Li and Outten, Iron–sulfur cluster exchange and Aft2 (2019) University of South Carolina research profile

title: Marc Solioz
desc: Investigated the copper-handling cop operon in Enterococcus hirae, including the CopY repressor, CopZ chaperone and CopA/CopB ATPases. This work helped connect copper transport, intracellular delivery and gene regulation. The linked publication documents his research at Bern. Copper Chaperones Gene regulation Connected copper delivery to bacterial gene control Solioz helped turn copper homeostasis into a connected molecular system through work on Enterococcus hirae. A collaborative study showed that the copper chaperone CopZ delivers copper to the CopY regulator, changing its association with DNA. Copper routing could therefore be linked directly to the regulation of copper-handling genes. His contribution explains how a microbe interprets and responds to a metal exposure. The biological effect depends on intracellular delivery and regulation as well as the amount outside the cell. That distinction is essential when studying copper contamination, copper-containing materials, or differences in microbial tolerance. The field now needs to connect these molecular responses to mixed communities and realistic exposure histories, rather than inferring ecological outcomes from a single organism’s tolerance. Cobine and colleagues, Copper delivery from CopZ to CopY (1999) Solioz and Stoyanov, Copper homeostasis in Enterococcus hirae (2003)

title: Andreas J. Bäumler
desc: Studies the ecological and metabolic mechanisms that allow enteric pathogens to colonize the intestine. His work connects inflammation, nutrient availability and bacterial competition, helping explain why Salmonella and related organisms can expand when gut conditions change. Salmonella Gut microbiome Inflammation Explaining how inflammation changes the microbial habitat Bäumler’s work established mechanisms through which intestinal inflammation changes microbial competition, including altered respiratory resources and host nutrient-withholding responses. This connected pathogen expansion to changes in the gut environment itself, rather than explaining dysbiosis only through the presence or absence of particular bacterial species. His contribution gives microbial metallomics an ecological framework: metal access operates inside a habitat whose oxygen, electron acceptors and nutrients also change. It helps investigators avoid assigning a community shift to a metal alone when the same inflammatory process has changed several resources at once. The frontier is to separate these interacting environmental drivers in human disease and determine which changes sustain dysbiosis, rather than merely accompanying the inflammatory response. UC Davis — Bäumler research: host inflammation and microbial ecology

title: Nigel J. Robinson
desc: Leading theorist of protein "metalation" — how cells ensure each metalloprotein gets the correct metal — and of metal-sensing regulators such as the nickel sensor InrS. Metalation Metal sensors Nickel Made available metal quantitatively distinguishable from total metal Robinson and colleagues used bacterial metal sensors to define the intracellular availability of different elements in thermodynamic terms. Comparing those values with a protein’s metal affinities explained how a cobalt-requiring enzyme can receive cobalt even when other metals bind more tightly in isolated biochemical measurements. This supplies a quantitative foundation for the atlas’s central distinction: a metal can be present without being available to a particular protein. It also makes mismetallation testable. The relevant comparison is between competing intracellular metal pools and protein affinities, rather than between dietary dose and a presumed biological effect. A major frontier is extending calibrated measurements of metal availability across species and physiological states, then testing whether they predict protein occupancy in complex host-associated communities. Osman and colleagues, Bacterial sensors and correct enzyme metalation (2019)

title: Barry P. Rosen
desc: Studies how organisms transport, transform and detoxify arsenic and other metals. His work on arsenic uptake, efflux, biomethylation and organoarsenical chemistry links bacterial resistance mechanisms to environmental exposure. FIU records his retirement in 2025. Arsenic Detoxification Transport Made arsenic exposure a question of cellular handling Rosen’s work maps how organisms admit, export, and transform arsenic. With colleagues, he demonstrated that the bacterial glycerol channel GlpF also permits entry of trivalent arsenic and antimony, while a separate transport system supports their removal. Environmental contamination thus meets specific cellular pathways, not an inert biological surface. For microbial metallomics, this turns a total arsenic result into a set of consequential questions: which chemical species is present, which organisms encounter it, and how do they handle it? His research connects environmental exposure to microbial physiology and helps explain why resistance, accumulation, and toxicity are different outcomes. An important frontier is determining how these cellular pathways collectively alter arsenic speciation and host exposure in intact communities, where competing transformations may occur simultaneously. FIU research profile Meng, Liu and Rosen, Arsenic and antimony transport (2004)

title: Lena J. Daumann
desc: A leader in lanthanide microbiology; characterized how methylotrophic and methanotrophic bacteria use rare-earth elements as catalytic cofactors in methanol dehydrogenase. Lanthanides Methylotrophs Enzymes Expanded the biological periodic table to rare-earth chemistry Daumann’s work examines why certain bacteria use lanthanides in alcohol-metabolizing enzymes. Her group compared how different lanthanide ions affect a bacterial methanol dehydrogenase, linking differences in catalytic activity to the elements’ coordination chemistry. Closely related rare-earth elements proved biologically distinguishable rather than interchangeable members of one chemical category. Her contribution broadens what microbial metallomics must look for. Elements with no established human nutritional requirement can still support microbial metabolism and environmental carbon cycling. That matters when interpreting emerging contaminants or microbial community function: the human nutrient list is not a complete map of biologically consequential metals. An important frontier is connecting enzyme-level lanthanide preferences to metal availability and metabolic activity in natural communities, especially where human activity changes rare-earth exposure. Lumpe and colleagues, Lanthanide identity and methanol dehydrogenase activity (2018) HHU Bioinorganic Chemistry laboratory

title: Kevin J. Waldron
desc: Studies how metalloproteins acquire the correct metal and how metal specificity evolves. Current laboratory work includes superoxide dismutases, bacterial metal homeostasis and the consequences of metal starvation for enzyme function. Metal specificity Superoxide dismutase Evolution Showed why metal deprivation can meet metabolic flexibility Waldron and collaborators demonstrated that a Staphylococcus aureus antioxidant enzyme can function with either iron or manganese. Their biochemical and infection-model evidence connected this cofactor flexibility to survival during host-imposed manganese restriction. The work explains an organism’s response to nutritional immunity at the level of enzyme function. This is important for microbiome medicine because an organism’s metal requirement may be conditional. Lowering one metal does not necessarily remove the function that depends on it under ordinary conditions. Waldron’s work makes metabolic flexibility part of evaluating metal-directed interventions and interpreting microbial responses to an inflamed environment. A next step is establishing how widespread functional cofactor flexibility is in host-associated communities, and when it changes responses to metal deprivation in clinically relevant settings. Garcia and colleagues, Cofactor flexibility and nutritional immunity (2017) IBB PAS, Laboratory of Metalloprotein Biology

title: Joseph A. Caruso †
desc: Advanced elemental speciation and ICP-MS-based metallomics through analytical methods that connect chromatography with mass spectrometry. His work helped make it possible to ask which chemical forms of metals occur in biological samples, rather than measuring total elemental abundance alone. ICP-MS Speciation Analytical chemistry Making metal speciation an analytical discipline Caruso advanced the coupling of chemical separations with element-sensitive mass spectrometry, including influential work on arsenic and selenium species. He also helped establish the journal Metallomics. His contribution supplied both analytical methods and a scholarly home for studying the biological meaning of particular metal-containing compounds. Total elemental content cannot reveal every difference between a nutrient, a transformed metabolite and a toxic species. Caruso’s legacy helps make those differences experimentally accessible, providing part of the measurement foundation needed to evaluate foods, microbial transformations and exposure claims in this field. The continuing task is reliable speciation in complex samples: preserving compounds during analysis, quantifying recovery and showing which measured species are relevant to biological exposure. RSC — Joseph Anthony Caruso: scientific and editorial contributions

title: Thomas E. Kehl-Fie
desc: Investigates how host-imposed nutrient starvation changes bacterial infection. His laboratory studies adaptations that allow Staphylococcus aureus to overcome metal restriction, and how nutritional immunity changes susceptibility to host defenses and antibiotics. Nutritional immunity Metal starvation Staphylococcus Showing why metal starvation can change antibiotic performance Kehl-Fie’s research connects host-imposed metal starvation to bacterial physiology. In a collaborative 2026 study, calprotectin-mediated zinc restriction reduced β-lactam killing of Staphylococcus aureus in laboratory and mouse experiments. This linked an immune defense to antibiotic tolerance, distinct from inherited antibiotic resistance. This is a consequential complication for antimicrobial development: an intervention that restricts an essential nutrient may have different effects on bacterial growth and antibiotic killing. Microbial metallomics therefore helps explain why the host environment belongs in the assessment of a proposed treatment. The clinical question is whether local metal availability helps explain treatment outcomes in people, and how that information can improve therapy without undermining nutritional immunity. Velez et al. — Calprotectin and β-lactam bactericidal activity University of Iowa — Understanding how starvation shapes infection

title: Uwe Karst
desc: Develops analytical methods for metal speciation and chemical imaging of biological tissues. His group combines laser-ablation ICP-MS, electrochemistry and mass spectrometry to investigate the distribution and transformation of metals and metal-containing compounds. LA-ICP-MS Metal imaging Speciation Joining the questions of where a metal is and what form it takes Karst develops methods for chemical imaging and elemental speciation, combining complementary approaches to map elements and identify metal-containing compounds. His group’s work includes biological tissues and the environmental fate of medical contrast agents, connecting spatial distribution with chemical identity rather than relying on a bulk measurement alone. For microbial metallomics, these are the tools needed to investigate local exposure. A whole-tissue average can hide a concentrated interface or redistribution between compartments. Imaging and speciation offer different pieces of that problem, helping distinguish where an element accumulates from what it may be doing there. The frontier is to align elemental maps with microbial location and molecular identity while controlling sample-preparation artifacts, so apparent colocalization can be tested as a functional interaction. University of Münster — Karst research: imaging and speciation

title: Karen Pendergrass
desc: Karen Pendergrass investigates upstream metal contamination in food systems and agricultural inputs, and how these exposures may influence microbial metabolism and disease. Her work connects exposure pathways with mismetallation and metal-dependent enzyme function, with particular attention to nickel, urease, [NiFe]-hydrogenases, and nickel-dependent forms of glyoxalase I. By examining microbiome and metallomic signatures together, she explores how changes in metal availability and enzyme activity may link microbial communities and heavy-metal exposure to conditions such as endometriosis and Parkinson’s disease. Microbial metallomics Heavy metal exposure Microbiome medicine Food & agricultural contamination Mismetallation Nickel & microbial enzymes Microbiome & metallomic signatures Heavy metals, microbes & microbiome medicine Pendergrass develops research frameworks that connect heavy metal exposure, metal-dependent microbial functions, and disease-associated microbiome signatures. Her 2025 Beneficial Microbes Conference presentation examined these connections in endometriosis through metallomics and nutritional immunity. Her subsequent writing applies related questions to Parkinson’s disease, metabolic health, and early-life exposure. Alongside this hypothesis-driven work, she designed the Heavy Metal Index’s evidence architecture and contributes to contaminant standards at ICS. Microbial metallomics asks what a metal does within a living system, rather than stopping at its measured concentration. Pendergrass’s contribution is to connect that question with both microbial-signature research and traceable exposure evidence. A food contaminant, a microbial enzyme, and a disease-associated community pattern can then be examined as parts of a proposed causal chain. The result is a set of specific mechanisms and research questions, with exposure standards grounded in a separately documented evidence base. The next question is which measured changes in metal form and availability explain microbial function in a particular tissue or community. Pairing exposure measurements with enzyme activity and microbiome data would help distinguish a causal metal–microbe relationship from an association, and identify which predictions from these frameworks hold up in independent studies.
