title: Kenneth H. Nealson
desc: Studies microbial physiology, environmental microbiology and the genomics of natural populations. His foundational work on metal-reducing bacteria helped establish Shewanella as a model for extracellular electron transfer and microbial fuel cells. Shewanella Metal reduction Microbial fuel cells Establishing that microbes can grow by reducing metal minerals Myers and Nealson demonstrated microbial growth coupled to manganese-oxide reduction in the organism now known as Shewanella oneidensis MR-1. This foundational work showed that a solid metal oxide can participate directly in microbial energy metabolism, helping make metal-reducing bacteria central models in environmental microbiology. The importance is broader than an unusual metabolic trait: microorganisms can change the chemical conditions that govern metal mobility and exposure. His work helps explain why predicting contamination requires attention to biological activity, and why some metals are microbial respiratory resources as well as nutrients or toxicants. The continuing challenge is to predict when metal-transforming activity in complex environments increases mobility, promotes immobilization, or changes exposure to organisms downstream in the ecosystem. Myers and Nealson — Bacterial manganese reduction and growth USC — Kenneth Nealson

title: Elizabeth M. Nolan
desc: Investigates the chemical competition for metals between hosts and microbes. Her work examines antimicrobial metal sequestration by calprotectin, bacterial siderophores and metallophores, and strategies for using iron-acquisition pathways to deliver antibiotics. Calprotectin Siderophores Nutritional immunity Expanding nutritional immunity from metal names to chemical forms Nolan’s group demonstrated that calprotectin can sequester ferrous iron and that this iron restriction contributes to bacterial growth inhibition. By identifying an unusual iron-binding site and its chemical behavior, the work expanded a protein chiefly associated with zinc and manganese withholding into a broader metal-defense mechanism. Her contribution explains why oxidation state and binding chemistry belong in microbiome medicine. An iron measurement does not establish which iron pool a host protein can capture or a microbe can use. That distinction connects coordination chemistry to competition at the host–microbe interface. The frontier is to determine when this chemistry controls microbial access in human tissues, and how metal-acquisition pathways might support selective antimicrobial delivery. Nakashige et al. — Human calprotectin is an iron-sequestering host-defense protein

title: Eric P. Skaar
desc: Investigates the struggle between hosts and pathogens for essential nutrients. His laboratory studies bacterial metal acquisition, the action of host metal-binding proteins such as calprotectin, and the metabolic adaptations that support infection. Nutritional immunity Staphylococcus Metal acquisition Making metal withholding visible at the site of infection Skaar and collaborators demonstrated that calprotectin accumulates in staphylococcal abscesses and restricts nutrient metals there. Their animal work connected the chemistry of the infected tissue to bacterial growth, helping establish manganese and zinc sequestration as components of nutritional immunity alongside iron restriction. For microbial metallomics, this changes the unit of analysis: the relevant environment is the metal pool a microbe encounters inside a particular tissue. It makes metal trafficking a concrete antimicrobial research target and gives metal measurements a direct connection to host defense. The translational question is which microbial metal dependencies remain vulnerable in human infection while preserving host metal requirements and the functions of beneficial communities. Corbin et al. — Metal chelation and inhibition of bacterial growth in tissue abscesses Skaar laboratory — Research mission

title: Jeffrey A. Gralnick
desc: Investigates extracellular electron transfer in Shewanella and related microbes. Work on secreted flavins, electron-transfer machinery and bacterial physiology connects basic microbial metabolism with metal reduction and applied biotechnology. Shewanella Flavins Electron transfer Revealing the molecules that connect microbes to external metals Gralnick and collaborators demonstrated that Shewanella releases flavins that mediate extracellular electron transfer. Subsequent work connected this activity to the organism’s respiratory machinery. These studies explain how microbial metabolism can reach beyond the cell and affect external minerals or conductive surfaces. For microbial metallomics, this supplies a mechanism between a microbe’s presence and a change in metal chemistry. It also shows why extracellular metabolites belong in measurements of microbial metal handling: interactions can occur through mobile molecules rather than requiring every cell to touch a mineral. The next measurement problem is to determine which extracellular pathways carry meaningful electron flow in mixed communities and how that activity changes metal fate under environmental conditions. Marsili et al. — Shewanella secretes flavins that mediate extracellular electron transfer University of Minnesota — Gralnick research profile

title: Amy C. Rosenzweig
desc: Investigates metalloprotein function with structural, spectroscopic, biochemical and genetic methods. Major interests include biological methane oxidation, oxygen activation, metal uptake and transport, and the biosynthesis of metal-binding natural products. Copper Methanotrophs Structural biology Shows metal enzymes working in their biological surroundings Rosenzweig’s group connects metalloprotein structure with chemical function. In a study of bacterial methane oxidation, examining particulate methane monooxygenase in a lipid environment restored activity and revealed previously unresolved structural features, including a copper-binding site. The work showed how the surrounding membrane can change the interpretation of an enzyme. This matters beyond one copper enzyme: microbial metal function cannot always be reconstructed from an isolated protein stripped of its surroundings. Her work links metal chemistry to microbial carbon cycling and provides a standard for validating function before making claims about environmental activity or a proposed biological application. A continuing challenge is to establish metal occupancy and catalytic behavior in intact organisms and communities, where membranes, metal supply, and environmental conditions act together. Koo and colleagues, Active methane monooxygenase in a lipid bilayer (2022) Northwestern research profile

title: Derek R. Lovley
desc: Studies the physiology and ecology of anaerobic microorganisms. Work on Geobacter and extracellular electron transfer connects metal reduction with groundwater bioremediation, microbial fuel cells and the development of biological electronic materials. Geobacter Bioremediation Electron transfer Showing that microbial metabolism can immobilize a contaminant Lovley and colleagues demonstrated that iron-reducing microorganisms can obtain energy through uranium reduction, converting soluble oxidized uranium into a less soluble reduced form. His wider work on Geobacter connects anaerobic metabolism and extracellular electron transfer to the movement and retention of metals in contaminated environments. This is a foundation for considering microbes as determinants of exposure, not merely organisms damaged by it. His contribution gives bioremediation a mechanistic basis: a microbial community can alter a contaminant’s chemical form and mobility, potentially changing what reaches water supplies and other biological systems. The practical frontier is durable containment: establishing whether a reduced metal remains immobilized as oxygen, hydrology and community activity change over time at a contaminated site. Lovley et al. — Microbial reduction of uranium UMass Amherst — Derek Lovley

title: Christopher Rensing
desc: Studies metal–microbe interactions across environmental and medical settings. His research connects bacterial metal resistance with electromicrobiology and bioremediation. ASM identifies him as a distinguished professor and director of the Institute of Environmental Microbiology at FAFU. Metal resistance Bioremediation Electromicrobiology Identified transport mechanisms that turn exposure into tolerance Rensing, Mitra, and Rosen demonstrated that the bacterial protein ZntA uses cellular energy to transport zinc and cadmium. This work connected metal tolerance to a defined transport function. Rensing’s broader research carries that mechanistic perspective across environmental microbiology, metal resistance, and the biological handling of contaminated environments. His contribution makes exposure assessment more biologically specific. Organisms sharing the same metal-containing environment may maintain different intracellular burdens because their transport systems differ. For microbial metallomics, that helps explain ecological selection and why external metal concentration alone cannot establish either microbial injury or the fate of a contaminant. The frontier is connecting measured transport activity to community changes under realistic mixtures and exposure durations, including determining when tolerance changes environmental metal mobility. Rensing, Mitra and Rosen, ZntA metal transport (1997) American Society for Microbiology profile

title: Detlef Günther
desc: A leading developer of laser-ablation ICP-MS instrumentation and imaging methods that underpin spatially resolved elemental and metallomic analysis. LA-ICP-MS Elemental imaging Instrumentation Building the instruments that make local metal distributions measurable Günther’s research advances laser-ablation ICP-MS and related approaches for trace-element analysis. His work on sample introduction, particle behavior and detection supports spatially resolved multielement measurements, addressing the instrumental limitations that determine whether a small metal-rich region can be distinguished from its surrounding material. This enables the field to ask where metals are distributed within a sample instead of collapsing everything into one average. For microbial metallomics, such capabilities can support studies of heterogeneous tissues, biofilms and environmental materials, provided the elemental maps are connected to appropriate biological measurements. The next challenge is quantitative comparability across sample types and laboratories, together with the spatial resolution and biological registration needed to interpret a measured metal distribution. ETH Zurich — Günther research and instrumentation

title: Amit R. Reddi
desc: Investigates the cellular mechanisms that activate metalloproteins and regulate their signaling functions. His laboratory focuses on heme trafficking and copper/zinc superoxide dismutase, using chemical biology to connect metal availability with metabolism and disease. Heme Metal sensors Redox biology Made mobile heme pools visible inside cells Reddi and colleagues developed fluorescent sensors that distinguish exchangeable heme from the larger total heme pool. In yeast, these tools revealed different heme availability across cellular compartments and linked a familiar metabolic protein, GAPDH, to heme buffering. Heme could be studied as a dynamic resource as well as an enzyme cofactor. This gives microbial metallomics a way to ask what a cell can actually use. A total iron or heme measurement cannot establish availability at a particular destination. Reddi’s measurement tools help connect metal allocation to metabolism and signaling, which is necessary for separating abundance from functional sufficiency. The next question is how exchangeable heme changes across host-associated organisms and stress states, and which measurements can link those changes to specific biological outcomes. Hanna and colleagues, Fluorescent sensors reveal heme dynamics (2016) Georgia Tech research profile

title: Robert J. P. Williams †
desc: Helped establish bioinorganic chemistry and the Irving–Williams stability series. His work connected metal coordination, enzyme function and biological evolution, providing a chemical foundation for understanding why cells use particular elements. Coordination chemistry Metalloenzymes Evolution Explained the chemical competition behind metal selection Williams helped establish how metal coordination governs biological function. With Harry Irving, he described a recurring order of stability among transition-metal complexes. His work connected such chemical preferences to metalloenzymes, making the identity and binding environment of a metal central to explanations of catalysis. This foundation explains why having enough metal is insufficient: a competing element may bind where another is needed. Microbial metallomics therefore has to examine chemical competition and cellular control together. Mismetallation becomes a mechanistic question about an enzyme’s occupancy and activity, rather than a vague claim of metal toxicity. The next step in applying this foundation is to establish which proteins acquire the wrong metal under real exposure conditions, and whether that change impairs function. Irving and Williams, The stability of transition-metal complexes (1953) Royal Society scientific profile

title: Michael D. L. Johnson
desc: Investigates how bacteria process, sense and maintain metals during infection. His laboratory connects microbial metal homeostasis with the host environment and potential antibacterial strategies, including the response of Streptococcus pneumoniae to copper. Copper Streptococcus Metal homeostasis Connecting copper toxicity to a specific metabolic failure Johnson and collaborators showed that excess copper disrupts aerobic nucleotide synthesis in Streptococcus pneumoniae, with evidence pointing to interference with a manganese-dependent pathway. The work separated this effect from a general oxidative-stress explanation and proposed mismetallation as a mechanism requiring further resolution. This makes metal toxicity a question of molecular function, not simply how much copper is present. For microbial metallomics, identifying the failed pathway is what can connect metal competition to microbial behavior and distinguish a plausible antibacterial mechanism from indiscriminate toxicity. The next challenge is to establish which metal–protein interactions dominate in relevant host environments and whether they can be targeted with acceptable selectivity and safety. Johnson, Kehl-Fie and Rosch — Copper intoxication and aerobic nucleotide synthesis University of Arizona — Johnson research profile

title: Dianne K. Newman
desc: Studies bioenergetics and the cell biology of metabolically diverse bacteria. Her work links electron transfer and redox-active metabolites with microbial communities, including biofilms in chronic infections and crop rhizospheres. Electron transfer Biofilms Geomicrobiology Connecting mineral chemistry to the physiology of biofilms Newman’s work connects microbial electron transfer with both environmental mineral transformations and chronic-infection biofilms. Her group showed that a redox-active phenazine can alter iron availability and support biofilm development in laboratory models, linking the chemical state of iron to collective microbial behavior. This brings a geobiological insight into medicine: microbes can modify the chemistry that governs their own access to resources. A contaminated environment or infected tissue is therefore an active reaction system, and its oxygen conditions and microbial metabolites can matter alongside total metal abundance. Translation requires establishing which redox processes are active in patient biofilms and whether changing those processes improves outcomes while protecting host tissue and microbial ecology.
